pages.title: US Hegemony and Hegemonic Stability Theory
pages.summary: Lists exam questions on hegemonic stability theory and the status of US hegemony, with the challenges of China, BRICS and NAM. Explains Kindleberger and Gilpin's theory that free trade needs a liberal economic order, which must be created and managed by a hegemon state or group of states.

pages.title: Qualities, span and examples of a Hegemon
pages.summary: A hegemon is a leader with capacity (economic and military power) and willingness, and the USA lacked willingness until after the Second World War. Hegemony lasts at most 100 years because of overstretch and free riders, with Pax Britannica and Pax Americana as the examples.

pages.title: US hegemony from Cold War to 2001
pages.summary: After the Second World War US hegemony was challenged by the Soviet Union and NAM, then by Japan and the EU (G7) and by the Vietnam defeat and overstretch. Since 1991 came the unipolar moment and Fukuyama's end of history, and since 2001 challenges from Islamic fundamentalism, China, Russia and BRICS, with North Korea the major irritant.

pages.title: Declinists in the US hegemony debate
pages.summary: Declinists include Fareed Zakaria (post-American world caused by the rise of others), Joseph Nye (Bush's reliance on hard power), Eric Edelman (shifting American spirit) and Niall Ferguson (a world without polarity). Madeleine Albright is the first anti-declinist, calling the US the indispensable nation.

pages.title: Anti-declinists and why China's rise worries
pages.summary: Huntington, Krauthammer and Mandelbaum argue that US power, choice and order sustain hegemony. On China, Nye, Mearsheimer and Graham Allison (Thucydides trap) see a threat because the speed and scale of its rise is unprecedented, as Lee Kuan Yew also stresses.

pages.title: Mearsheimer versus Kissinger; Tibet and Taiwan policy
pages.summary: Mearsheimer says the US must keep the power gap with China, while Kissinger urges respectful engagement. The page explains US containment tools, namely the Tibet Policy Act 2002 and Taiwan policy under the Shanghai Communique 1972 and the Taiwan Relations Act 1979, alongside high US-China interdependence.

pages.title: Taiwan call, Xinjiang, trade disputes, two schools
pages.summary: Notes the controversy over the US President's direct call to Taiwan's president against the one-China policy, US criticism over Uighurs, and trade disputes including a proposed 45% tariff. Lecture 21 (24/04/2017) then opens the question of whether China is a real threat: Mearsheimer and Allison urge containment, Kissinger engagement.

pages.title: US containment of China: Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang
pages.summary: To protect its hegemony the USA contains potential challengers by allying with Chinese neighbours and creating domestic issues for China. It follows one-China policy yet commits under the Taiwan Relations Act 1979, supports Tibet under the Tibet Policy Act 2002, and criticises human rights violations against Uighurs.

pages.title: Economic conflict and why war is unlikely
pages.summary: Economic friction includes a $350 bn US trade deficit, currency manipulation, IPR violation and dumping, plus China's role on North Korea, Iran, Syria and Russia. Conflict is unlikely because of economic interdependence and shared interests in North Korea, counter-terrorism, Afghanistan and climate talks.

pages.title: Is China a real threat? Two schools
pages.summary: Recommends that the USA treat China respectfully with engagement, not containment, and ensure its peaceful rise. The first school (Lee Kuan Yew) stresses China's exceptional rise, its economy surpassing the US by 2030 and AIIB and OBOR; the second sees no near threat because of China's unstable periphery, internal pressure, technology gap and weak soft power.

pages.title: China no real threat; NAM introduced
pages.summary: Concludes that China will grow old before it becomes big while the USA has a demographic dividend. Begins NAM as a challenge, listing exam questions and describing NAM as the largest developing-country platform outside the UNGA, born in the Cold War from leaders such as Nehru, Sukarno, Tito and Nasser.

flashcards.front: Who propounded Hegemonic Stability Theory and what is its core claim?
flashcards.back: Charles Kindleberger and Robert Gilpin. Free trade is vital for peace, but a liberal economic order does not emerge on its own; it must be created and managed by a hegemon, a state or group of states.

flashcards.front: What two qualities define a hegemon, and why is hegemony limited to about 100 years?
flashcards.back: A hegemon needs capacity (economic and military power) and willingness; the USA had capacity but lacked willingness until after the Second World War. Hegemony fades through hegemon overstretch and free riders.

flashcards.front: How was US hegemony challenged between the 1940s and the 1980s?
flashcards.back: After the Second World War it faced the Soviet Union and NAM; in the 1960s the rise of Japan and the EU led to the G7; in the 1970s and 80s the Vietnam defeat showed economic and military overstretch.

flashcards.front: Name the declinists in the US hegemony debate and the reason each gives.
flashcards.back: Zakaria: a post-American world caused by the rise of others; Nye: Bush's excessive reliance on hard power; Edelman: a shifting American spirit after economic downturn and counter-insurgency; Ferguson: a world with no polarity and diffused power.

flashcards.front: What do the anti-declinists Albright, Huntington, Krauthammer and Mandelbaum argue?
flashcards.back: Albright: the US is the indispensable nation; Huntington: its strategic location and capacity exceed any other country's; Krauthammer: decline is a choice that can be arrested; Mandelbaum: because the US exists there is order, and hence US hegemony.

flashcards.front: What is the Thucydides trap and how do Mearsheimer and Kissinger differ on China?
flashcards.back: Graham Allison's Thucydides trap says the US and China are bound for conflict. Mearsheimer, like Allison, urges containment and a preserved power gap, while Kissinger, architect of rapprochement, urges engagement and respectful treatment.

flashcards.front: What legal and policy commitments shape US containment through Taiwan and Tibet?
flashcards.back: The US follows one-China policy since the Shanghai Communique 1972, but the Taiwan Relations Act 1979 commits it to ensure integration is not by force. The Tibet Policy Act 2002 created a special coordinator and commits it to protect Tibet's heritage and promote dialogue.

flashcards.front: Why does the second school say China is no near threat to US hegemony?
flashcards.back: China lacks a peaceful periphery, is in a pressure-cooker of internal issues, cannot match US technology, is merely the world's factory with weak soft power, and may grow old before it becomes big, while the US has a demographic dividend.

answers.question: Critically examine the debate on the decline of US hegemony in the post-Cold War world order.
answers.intro: Kindleberger and Gilpin's Hegemonic Stability Theory holds that a liberal order needs a capable and willing hegemon. Since 1991 US hegemony has been contested, and scholars divide into declinists, who see decline, and anti-declinists, who deny it.
body: Challenges: even after 1945 hegemony was not absolute, as the Soviet Union and NAM challenged it; Japan and the EU rose in the 1960s, leading to the G7, and the Vietnam defeat showed overstretch in the 1970s and 80s.

Declinists: Fareed Zakaria argues we already live in a post-American world because others have risen; Joseph Nye blames Bush-era reliance on hard power; Eric Edelman cites a shifting American spirit after downturn and counter-insurgency; Niall Ferguson sees a world without polarity.

Anti-declinists: Madeleine Albright calls the US the indispensable nation; Huntington says its strategic location and capacity exceed any other state's; Krauthammer holds decline is a choice that can be arrested; Mandelbaum links US presence to world order itself.

Since 2001 challengers include Islamic fundamentalism, China, a resurgent Russia and BRICS, but the notes treat the Islamic threat as minor and BRICS as uncertain, leaving China, Russia and North Korea as the main irritants.
answers.conclusion: The evidence suggests US hegemony is contested rather than collapsed: relative power is diffusing, yet no rival matches its capacity. Its durability will depend on pairing capacity with willingness while avoiding the overstretch that ends hegemonies.

answers.question: Is China a real threat to US hegemony? Discuss with reference to the two schools of thought.
answers.intro: Scholars split on China: one school sees a rising challenger to be contained, the other advises engagement or sees no near threat. The notes show Washington pursuing both containment and engagement because US-China interdependence is very high.
body: Threat school: Mearsheimer warns the US must not let the power gap narrow; Graham Allison predicts a Thucydides trap; Lee Kuan Yew stresses the unprecedented speed of China's rise, and the Chinese economy may surpass the US by 2030 while AIIB and OBOR build a Sino-centric world.

Containment tools: alliances with Chinese neighbours; the one-China policy since the 1972 Shanghai Communique with the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act against forceful integration; the Tibet Policy Act 2002 with a special coordinator; and criticism over Uighur Muslims in Xinjiang.
Economic friction: a US trade deficit with China of $350 bn, charges of currency manipulation, IPR violation and dumping, and a Make in America and Invest in America policy.

No-near-threat school: China lacks a peaceful periphery, faces pressure-cooker internal issues, trails in technology, and is the world's factory with no soft-power match; it may grow old before becoming big, whereas the US has a demographic dividend.
Engagement case: Kissinger urges treating China respectfully; shared stakes exist in North Korea, counter-terrorism, Afghanistan and climate talks.
answers.conclusion: China is better seen as a long-term competitor than an immediate threat. The notes recommend engagement without containment, respect for China's aspirations, and ensuring its rise is peaceful, since economic interdependence makes outright conflict costly for both.
